sentences.text: Chilantaisaurus was a large theropod dinosaur that measured approximately 11 meters in length and weighed between 2.5 and 4 metric tons.
Some estimates suggest the animal could have reached lengths of 13 meters, though its mass remained within the 2.5 to 4 ton range.
A distinctive feature of this species is a crescent-shaped, pitted muscle scar located on the front surface of the upper arm bone's muscle attachment area.
The known forelimb bones include a humerus that ranks among the largest ever discovered in any theropod dinosaur.
Its hindlimbs were long and featured a robust metatarsus, which is the largest known among purported megaraptorans or Neovenator.
The type specimen includes a femur measuring 1.19 meters in length and a tibia measuring 954 millimeters.
The genus Chilantaisaurus was formally described by the Chinese paleontologist Hu Show-Yung in 1964.
Fossils were first uncovered in 1960 at the Tashuikou site in Inner Mongolia, China, by a joint Sino-Soviet expedition.
The holotype specimen was found by the same joint Sino-Soviet expedition within the Ulansuhai Formation.
Only a partial skull and a few vertebrae of Chilantaisaurus have been found to date.
In the same 1964 paper where he described C. tashuikouensis, Hu named the species Chilantaisaurus maortuensis.

It is debated whether Chilantaisaurus weighed about 6 metric tons; while some researchers estimate this based on femur length comparisons to Tyrannosaurus, others argue that femoral circumference relates to locomotor load capacity rather than body mass.
The original describer Hu classified Chilantaisaurus as a carnosaur, but this classification has been challenged by later studies.
In 1964, the genus was originally classified by Hu as a member of Carnosauria related to Allosaurus.
Hu classified the animal as a Megalosauridae, while Paul and Molnar later considered it a carnosaur within the paraphyletic Allosauria.
A 2010 study by Benson, Carrano, and Brusatte classified Chilantaisaurus as a member of the clade Neovenatoridae within Megaraptora.
In 2012, Allain and colleagues classified Chilantaisaurus within Spinosauridae based on traits such as a high humeral to femoral length ratio and an enlarged manual ungual.
The species C. maortuensis has been reclassified multiple times, moving from Alashansaurus to Shaochilong, where it is classified as a carcharodontosaurid.
The parent group of the genus is Neovenatoridae.
Chilantaisaurus fossils date to the Late Cretaceous period, specifically younger than approximately 92 million years ago.
The fossil range of Chilantaisaurus is the Upper Cretaceous.
The Ulansuhai Formation containing Chilantaisaurus fossils is estimated to date from the Santonian to Campanian stages, between 85.7 and 72.2 million years ago.
The environment where Chilantaisaurus lived was a floodplain characterized by meandering rivers, as indicated by the red mudstone and siltstone of the formation.
The Ulansuhai Formation, where Chilantaisaurus fossils were found, indicates a floodplain environment defined by meandering rivers.
If Chilantaisaurus is confirmed as a spinosaurid, it would represent one of the few spinosaurids found in Asia and potentially the youngest member of the clade.
The genus lived from the Turonian to the Santonian stages, approximately 93.9 to 83.6 million years ago.
There is an ongoing debate regarding the classification of Chilantaisaurus, with some studies placing it in Spinosauridae while others have not.
The exact age of the Ulansuhai Formation is currently debated among researchers.
Several fossils originally assigned to C. tashuikouensis by Hu are now considered indeterminate because they do not overlap with the main type material.
Recent studies suggest that C. zheziangensis is likely an indeterminate therizinosaur rather than a species of Chilantaisaurus.
Researchers Chure and Rauhut suggest that Ch. maortuensis is probably a ceratosaurian.
